newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, orange juice prices fall, nearby soy firm.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, orange juice prices fall, nearby soy firm.

text.p: Coffee prices fell on Friday as traders speculated that a monthly report on U.S. coffee stockpiles would show a large build-up in July.

In other markets, orange juice fell to new 4-1/2 year lows on an estimate for a record Florida crop, while futures prices for nearest-month deliveries of soybeans and gasoline rose on worries about available supplies.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for delivery in September closed 6.60 cents a pound lower at 177.95 cents ahead of a monthly stocks report from the Green Coffee Association of New York.
After the close, the group reported that U.S. warehouse stocks of coffee rose 219,000 bags last month from the June levels, to a total of 2,335,000 bags.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.
Trade guesses had ranged for a rise of 50,000 to as many as 250,000 bags following coffee imports last month as high prices drew in shipments to ease tight supplies.

"Basically, it was down on GCA. There is nervousness about how much supply there is," said Ann Prendergast, an analyst with Refco Inc. "An increase breaks a historical trend. Stocks have seasonally gone down in July for the last three years."
At the New York Cotton Exchange, orange juice futures sank to new 4-1/2-year lows as speculators sold heavily on the prospect of another record crop in Florida.

Frozen concentrated orange juice for November delivery closed down the 5.00 cent a pound allowable daily limit at 71.10 cents. September futures set a life-of-contract low at 67.50 cents a pound, the lowest price for an orange juice futures contract since 65.45 cents in February 1993.

Selling was heavy for a second straight day after traders said private forecaster Citrus Consulting International of Orlando, Florida, on Thursday estimated the coming Florida orange crop at a record 253 million 90-pound boxes.
That would would be a hefty 12 percent rise over Florida's record crop of 225.7 million boxes in the current year.

"Two hundred and fifty-three is a big number," said Jim Cordier, an analyst with Allendale Commodities. "For the most part, this market is terminal now. It is not going to be able to shake this number for a while."

Copper prices fell to six-month lows under the weight of sluggish industrial demand and rising warehouse stockpiles. Copper for September delivery at the COMEX closed 3.80 cents a pound lower at $1.00 a pound.
Traders cited steady exports of copper from Chile, Peru and Brazil. Stock levels at London Metal Exchange warehouses are at their highest levels since last September.

"We've seen a sharp increase in stocks," said Michael Frawley, senior vice president of Dean Witter Reynolds. "The summer doldrums are upon us. I would expect to see this market on the defensive for the next three to four weeks. After that, ultimately we're looking at a good buying opportunity."

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices closed lower on forecasts for beneficial rains in the Midwest through the weekend, which are expected to aid maturation of this year's crop. December corn closed 5-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $2.62-1/2.

Soybeans will also benefit from the rains, boosting potential supplies this fall. But prices on Friday continued to hold steady as traders focused on worries about the growing tightness of remaining supplies from last year's crop.
Soybeans for August delivery ended 19-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $7.91-3/4, while September soybeans closed up 1/2 cent a bushel at $6.56.
Some early-harvested soybeans will arrive in September.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline futures for September delivery also bucked the lower trend in oil markets and closed higher for a fifth straight day on supply concerns.

September gasoline closed 0.48 cent a gallon higher at 66.81 cents, the only gasoline contract to post a gain on the day. September crude oil eased 1 cent to $20.07 a barrel and September heating oil fell 0.62 cent a gallon to 55.25 cents.

Exxon Corp this week said its Baytown, Texas, refinery shut a 110,000 barrel-per-day gasoline-making catalytic cracker due to operational problems. Tosco Corp's Bayway refinery in Linden, New Jersey, had shut a similar 150,000 barrel a day unit last month but may restart it as early as this weekend.

"The gasoline buying argument is that the gasoline market is still quite tight. Exxon's Baytown is out of the market and Tosco's Bayway is too," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group in New York.
"You don't want to be short the market until there is confirmation that Bayway's cat cracker has restarted," he said.
